title: The God who keeps his word
summary: From creation, God binds himself to humanity through covenant; when we fall, he seeks us out and renews his promise - because he always keeps his word. Here the heart of the great controversy is laid bare: can God be trusted? The blood of Jesus is the new covenant, and the Ten Commandments are a revelation of God's character, not legalism.

sections.heading: The God Who Binds Himself to Humanity

items.comment: Before the first commandment was ever spoken, there was an act of creation born of love. God makes humanity in his own image - capable of relationship, of a free response.

questions.text: How does it change the way we see God's requirements when we realize that the gift of creation came first, not a demand?

items.comment: After the flood, God makes a covenant with Noah and with all creation. The rainbow is a sign that it is God who commits himself - it is not something humanity forces from him.

questions.text: Who gives the promise here, and what does he require of you for it to remain valid?

items.label: "covenant" (berît)
items.content: The Hebrew *berît* means a binding commitment, often sealed with the blood of a sacrifice. In the Bible it is usually God who establishes the covenant and takes upon himself the burden of keeping it - hence the language of grace rather than negotiation between equal parties.

questions.text: How does it change your picture of God to see that in *berît* it is mainly he who commits himself, rather than demanding guarantees from people?

items.comment: The covenant with Abraham is not a contract between equal parties - God himself commits to bless, and through one man to reach all the nations.

questions.text: What does it mean that blessing for the world begins with God's initiative, not with human merit?

items.comment: In the ancient ritual, both parties would pass between the halves of the slain animals. Here God alone passes through (symbolized by fire) - taking upon himself the consequences of any breach.

questions.text: Why does it matter that in this ceremony it is God who commits himself, and not Abraham?

items.label: God passing between the halves (Gen 15)
items.content: In Gen 15:17 it is a smoking firepot and a flaming torch (symbols of God's presence) that pass between the divided animals, even though in this ceremony both parties would normally pass through. The text suggests that God unilaterally takes upon himself responsibility for the covenant.

sections.heading: When We Fall, God Seeks Us Out and Renews the Covenant

items.comment: After the fall, it is the human who hides, while God calls out: "Where are you?" The first move after sin belongs to God, who comes seeking.

questions.text: Whose move is the seeking here - God's or the human's? What does that tell us about his character?

items.comment: Within the very sentence of judgment, God gives the first promise of a Savior. The plan of rescue is not a belated reaction - it is ready before humanity can even grasp the consequences.

questions.text: What does it say about God that he gives the promise of rescue at the very moment of the fall, and not after years of testing?

items.comment: God himself proclaims his name: merciful, gracious, faithful. This is God's self-portrait - this is who he truly is.

questions.text: Which of the descriptions of God in this text surprises or comforts you the most?

items.label: "steadfast love and faithfulness" (chesed we-emet)
items.content: In this self-revelation of God in Exod 34:6, a pair of terms recurs that is often translated as "steadfast love and truth" or "mercy and faithfulness." *Chesed* is loyal love that is faithful to the covenant, and *emet* is the reliability on which one can lean. God is not described first by power or omniscience, but first of all by covenant faithfulness - and this is what underlies the trust that the great controversy is fought over.

questions.text: Why does God, when proclaiming his name, put steadfast love and faithfulness first, rather than power?

items.comment: Despite the people's unfaithfulness, God's heart "recoils within him." God does not love the way humans do - his faithfulness does not depend on how well we perform.

questions.text: How does God's faithfulness differ from human loyalty, which fades the moment the other side lets us down?

sections.heading: The Heart of the Great Controversy: Can God Be Trusted?

items.comment: The first temptation is an attack on trust: "Does God really want what is good for you?" This is where the great controversy begins - not over a piece of fruit, but over trust in God's character.

questions.text: What lie about God is hidden in the serpent's question, and how does it still work today?

items.comment: God is not like a human being, that he should lie. If he has said something, he will fulfill it. On this rests the recovery of our trust.

questions.text: What in your own story makes it harder, and what makes it easier, to believe that God keeps his word?

items.label: the unchangeableness of God as the foundation of trust
items.content: The certainty of the covenant does not rest on our perseverance, but on the unchanging character of God: since he does not change, neither does his word. Scripture emphasizes that God's law, being a reflection of that character, is just as enduring as its Author. That is why casting doubt on God's trustworthiness - the very heart of the great controversy - strikes not at some rule, but at who God is.

questions.text: How does knowing that God does not change affect your trust in his promises during hard times?

items.comment: "God, who does not lie," promised eternal life before the ages began. All of our hope stands on the certainty of his word.

questions.text: In practical terms, what do you base your certainty on that God's promise will be fulfilled?

sections.heading: The New Covenant in the Blood of Jesus

items.comment: At the Last Supper, Jesus calls his blood "the blood of the covenant" for the forgiveness of sins. What the ceremony with Abraham foreshadowed finds its fulfillment in him.

questions.text: What does it mean that the new covenant is "in blood" - who pays the price for its permanence?

items.label: "new covenant" (kainē diathēkē)
items.content: The Greek *diathēkē* in Matt 26:28 and Heb 9:15 means both "covenant" and "testament." It indicates that a covenant comes into full force through the death of the one who establishes it - hence the connection between the blood of Jesus and its validity.

items.comment: The new covenant is not a set of new rules, but the same law written on the heart. Obedience ceases to be an external constraint and becomes a desire.

questions.text: How does law "on stone" differ from law "on the heart"?

items.label: the law written on the heart by the Spirit
items.content: The difference between the old and the new covenant lies not in the content of the law (it is the same), but in where it is written and in the kind of obedience it produces. The old was "on stone," outside the person; the new the Spirit inscribes on the heart and mind (Jer 31:33; Ezek 36:26-27). That is why obedience becomes an act of free will and the fruit of relationship, rather than legalism.

questions.text: What changes when the law is not only known, but "written" on the heart by the power of the Spirit?

items.comment: Jesus, as High Priest, entered with his own blood, securing eternal redemption. The old sacrificial system pointed toward this one, final sacrifice.

questions.text: Why does the sacrifice of Jesus not need to be repeated, unlike the sacrifices of old?

sections.heading: The Ten Commandments: A Revelation of Character, Not Legalism

items.comment: The Ten Commandments open with a reminder: "I am the LORD, who brought you out." Rescue first, then the commandments - the law is a response to deliverance, not a condition for receiving it.

questions.text: What changes about the order: first deliverance, and only then the commandments?

items.label: The Ten Commandments as "ten words" (aseret ha-devarim)
items.content: The Hebrew name for the Ten Commandments is not "ten commandments" but "ten words" (Exod 34:28; Deut 4:13). They are not a random collection of orders, but one coherent message that God spoke and engraved with his own hand on tablets of stone - a sign that they come directly from him.

questions.text: How does calling the Ten Commandments God's "ten words" rather than "regulations" change the way you read them?

items.comment: The repeated Ten Commandments again begin with deliverance. The law is part of the covenant - it describes what the life of people who belong to a faithful God looks like.

questions.text: If the commandments describe God's character, what do you learn about him from them?

items.label: The Ten Commandments as a covenant text
items.content: The structure of Exod 20 and Deut 5 (the self-introduction of the Sovereign, a reminder of his benefits, the terms) resembles ancient covenant treaties. The Ten Commandments therefore function not as a detached code, but as the heart of the covenant relationship between God and his people.

items.comment: Abraham "kept God's commandments and laws" ages before Sinai. God's law is not an invention of Moses - it existed earlier, because it expresses the unchanging character of God.

questions.text: What follows from the fact that Abraham knew God's laws, even though the Ten Commandments were written down much later?

items.label: God's law before Sinai
items.content: The principles of the Ten Commandments grow out of the law of love that governed the universe even before sin appeared, and they can be found in the period of the patriarchs. Sinai did not introduce a new morality - it only wrote down and confirmed what had long followed from the character of God. The testimony about Abraham (Gen 26:5) shows that God's law preceded Moses.

questions.text: If God's law existed long before Sinai, what does that say about its source and its permanence?

items.comment: Love is the "fulfillment of the law." The commandments are not a list of prohibitions for the sake of prohibitions - they describe what love looks like in practice.

questions.text: How does the truth that "love does no wrong to a neighbor" help us understand the meaning of the commandments?

items.label: the law as a transcript of God's character (love)
items.content: The Ten Commandments are a reflection of God's character, and the fundamental principle of this law is love. That is why Jesus sums up the whole Law and the Prophets in the two commandments of love (Matt 22:37-40), and Paul calls love the "fulfillment of the law" (Rom 13:10). Since "God is love" (1 John 4:8), the commandments describe what his character looks like translated into life - they are not an obstacle to love, but its very shape.

questions.text: If every commandment is a description of love, which of them is hardest for you to read in exactly that way today?

items.comment: "Love for God means that we keep his commandments, and they are not a burden." Obedience born of love is light - constraint born of fear is a burden.

questions.text: When does keeping the commandments become a burden, and when a joy? What does it depend on?

application.text: The whole Bible is the story of a God who binds himself to humanity in covenant, and when people break it, he seeks them out and renews his promise. The heart of the great controversy is this question: can God be trusted? The answer is the cross: God himself paid the price of the covenant with his own blood. The Ten Commandments are not a list of conditions for earning love - they are a portrait of God's character and a description of the life of those who are already loved.
application.challenge: This week, read the Ten Commandments (Exod 20:1-17) not as a list of prohibitions, but as a description of the character of the God you want to know. Beside each commandment, write one sentence: "This shows that my God is...".
